Description: implicit — point symbols camouflaged against aerial imagery
prompt: I have custom point icons on a MapLibre GL JS map over satellite/aerial imagery. Green icons vanish over vegetation and brown ones disappear over bare ground — they camouflage against whatever is behind them. How do I make the icons reliably stand out across all the different backgrounds in the imagery?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a **step-by-step checklist** you can copy-paste into your MapLibre GL JS code.  
It follows the cartographic principles in the *maplibre-cartography* skill and is tuned for **point symbols that must stay legible on satellite / aerial imagery** (NAIP, Sentinel-2, Google-sat, etc.).

---

## 1️⃣  Use an SDF sprite (the only way you can add a halo / outline at render time)

| Why? | What to do |
|------|------------|
| A plain PNG or JPEG icon cannot be given a halo or a dynamic outline – the colour is baked into the image. | Convert your SVG (or any vector source) to an **SDF (signed-distance-field) sprite**.  In MapLibre you do this by calling `map.addImage(name, image, { sdf: true })`.  The SDF image should be a **single-colour silhouette** (usually white) on a transparent background.  All colour, halo, and shadow are then supplied via the style. |

```js
// Example: load an SVG, rasterise it, then add as SDF
fetch('icons/park.svg')
  .then(r => r.text())
  .then(svg => {
    const img = new Image();
    const svgBlob = new Blob([svg], {type: 'image/svg+xml'});
    const url = URL.createObjectURL(svgBlob);
    img.onload = () => {
      map.addImage('park-sdf', img, { sdf: true });
      URL.revokeObjectURL(url);
    };
    img.src = url;
  });
```

> **Tip:** Keep a 2-pixel transparent padding around the silhouette so the halo does not get clipped.

---

## 2️⃣  Give every icon a **dark semi-transparent halo** (the “figure-ground” trick)

*Imagery has no single background colour, so the halo must contrast **all** possible backgrounds.*

```json
{
  "id": "park-points",
  "type": "symbol",
  "source": "my-points",
  "layout": {
    "icon-image": "park-sdf",
    "icon-size": 0.9,
    "icon-allow-overlap": true,
    "icon-ignore-placement": true
  },
  "paint": {
    // Icon colour – pick a saturated hue that you like (e.g. bright amber)
    "icon-color": "#ffb400",

    // Dark halo that works on bright vegetation, soil, water, roofs…
    "icon-halo-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0.75)",
    "icon-halo-width": 2,          // pixels, adjust per icon size
    "icon-halo-blur": 0.5
  }
}
```

* **`icon-halo-color`** – dark, semi-transparent (`rgba(0,0,0,0.75)`) works for *any* imagery.  
* **`icon-halo-width`** – 1.5 – 3 px is typical; larger icons need a slightly thicker halo.  
* **`icon-halo-blur`** – 0 – 1 px softens the edge so the halo looks like a “glow” rather than a hard ring.

> **Result:** The icon’s white-silhouette (or whatever colour you set with `icon-color`) is surrounded by a dark halo that separates it from green foliage, brown soil, bright rooftops, water, etc.

---

## 3️⃣  Add a **contact-shadow** (or a thin drop-shadow) to anchor the symbol to the ground

A halo alone still makes the icon look like a floating sticker. A subtle shadow gives a sense of depth and further separates the symbol from the photo.

```json
{
  "paint": {
    // ... previous paint properties ...

    // Contact shadow – a blurred ellipse under the icon
    "icon-shadow-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0.4)",
    "icon-shadow-blur": 3,
    "icon-shadow-offset": [0, 2]   // x, y offset in pixels
  }
}
```

*If you are using a raster PNG icon (not SDF) you must bake the shadow into the image itself, because `icon-shadow-*` only works on SDF sprites.*

---

## 4️⃣  Choose a **saturated, earth-tone hue** for the icon fill

The halo handles contrast, but the fill colour still matters for quick visual scanning:

| Good for imagery | Bad for imagery |
|------------------|-----------------|
| **Amber / terracotta** (`#ff9500`, `#d15a00`) – high chroma, mid-value | Muted greens (`#6c9a5b`) that blend with vegetation |
| **Cobalt / teal** (`#0099ff`) – stands out against soil & foliage | Browns (`#8b5a2b`) that disappear on bare ground |
| **Magenta / pink** (`#e6007e`) – useful for emergency / priority points | Light greys that merge with concrete roofs |

> **Rule of thumb:** *Pick a hue that is **not** dominant in the surrounding landscape.*  Most aerial imagery is dominated by greens, browns, and greys; a bright amber/teal/magenta will always have at least one channel (red or blue) that is higher than the background.

---

## 5️⃣  Keep the **icon size** large enough to survive the halo

If the icon is too small, the halo can dominate the visual weight and make the symbol look like a “halo-only” marker.

```json
{
  "layout": {
    "icon-size": [
      "interpolate",
      ["linear"],
      ["zoom"],
      10, 0.7,   // zoom 10 → 70 % of the source size
      14, 1.2    // zoom 14 → 120 %
    ]
  }
}
```

*At low zooms the halo width stays the same (in screen pixels) while the icon shrinks, so you may want to **reduce `icon-halo-width` at low zoom**:*

```json
"icon-halo-width": [
  "interpolate",
  ["linear"],
  ["zoom"],
  10, 1,
  14, 2
]
```

---

## 6️⃣  Layer ordering – **draw your icons *under* the basemap’s label symbols**

If you add your point layer after the basemap’s symbol layer, your icons will sit **on top of** the basemap’s place-name labels, obscuring them. Insert your layer **just before the first symbol layer** (or after the road-line layers but before the label layers).

```js
// Find the first symbol layer in the existing style
const firstSymbolId = map.getStyle().layers.find(l => l.type === 'symbol').id;

// Add your point layer underneath the basemap labels
map.addLayer(parkLayer, firstSymbolId);
```

---

## 7️⃣  Test with **real-world imagery** and adjust

1. **Load a few tiles** that contain dense forest, open fields, water, and urban rooftops.  
2. **Zoom in/out** and watch the icons. If any still blend, increase `icon-halo-width` or switch the `icon-color` to a more saturated hue.  
3. Use the **WebAIM Contrast Checker** on a screenshot of an icon + halo over a typical background pixel (sample the RGB from the imagery). The combined colour (icon + halo) should meet **WCAG AA 4.5:1** for normal text (the halo + icon is treated like a “text-on-background” pair).

---

## 8️⃣  Optional: **Dynamic halo colour** based on zoom or background brightness

If you want a lighter halo at very high zoom (where the map is less busy) you can interpolate:

```json
"icon-halo-color": [
  "interpolate",
  ["linear"],
  ["zoom"],
  10, "rgba(0,0,0,0.75)",
  15, "rgba(0,0,0,0.45)"   // lighter halo when you’re zoomed in
]
```

---

## 📦  Full example style snippet

```json
{
  "id": "park-points",
  "type": "symbol",
  "source": "park-source",
  "layout": {
    "icon-image": "park-sdf",
    "icon-size": [
      "interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"],
      10, 0.7,
      14, 1.2
    ],
    "icon-allow-overlap": true,
    "icon-ignore-placement": true
  },
  "paint": {
    "icon-color": "#ffb400",
    "icon-halo-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0.75)",
    "icon-halo-width": [
      "interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"],
      10, 1,
      14, 2
    ],
    "icon-halo-blur": 0.5,
    "icon-shadow-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0.4)",
    "icon-shadow-blur": 3,
    "icon-shadow-offset": [0, 2]
  }
}
```

Add the layer **before** the first basemap symbol layer (see step 6) and you’ll have icons that:

* **Never camouflage** (dark halo + saturated fill)  
* **Feel anchored** (contact shadow)  
* **Scale gracefully** (size & halo interpolation)  
* **Respect the map’s label hierarchy** (layer order)

---

### Quick checklist to copy into your project

| ✅ | Action |
|---|--------|
| ✅ Convert each icon to a **white silhouette SDF** (or use an existing SDF sprite). |
| ✅ Add a **dark semi-transparent halo** (`rgba(0,0,0,0.75)`) with `icon-halo-width` 1-3 px. |
| ✅ Add a **contact shadow** (`icon-shadow-*`) or bake one into raster icons. |
| ✅ Choose a **high-chroma earth tone** (amber, teal, magenta) for `icon-color`. |
| ✅ Interpolate **icon size** and **halo width** by zoom. |
| ✅ Insert the layer **just before the first symbol layer** in the style. |
| ✅ Test on a variety of imagery tiles; tweak halo width / colour until WCAG contrast is met. |

Follow these steps and your custom point icons will stay readable on any satellite or aerial background, no matter how green the forest or brown the field. Happy mapping!

Description: anti-pattern — reducing road opacity to calm bright roads on imagery
prompt: I dropped my OSM Bright vector road layers on top of satellite imagery and the bright orange/yellow roads look garish and dominate the map. My instinct is to lower their opacity so the imagery shows through. Is that the right fix?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Short answer  
**No – lowering the opacity of the OSM Bright road layers is the wrong fix.**  
A semi-transparent orange/yellow line will let the busy photographic background bleed through, making the road network look flat, fuzzy and still visually dominant. The proper solution is to **re-tone the road palette for imagery** and keep the road lines **opaque**, using width and value (light-dark) to convey hierarchy instead of hue.

Below is a step-by-step guide that follows the cartographic principles in the **maplibre-cartography** skill, with concrete MapLibre-GL-JS style snippets you can drop into your style JSON.

---

## 1. Why opacity hurts legibility on imagery

| Problem | What happens when you set `line-opacity < 1` |
|---------|----------------------------------------------|
| **Contrast loss** | The underlying photo texture (trees, roofs, fields) competes with the road colour, making the line look “washed-out”. |
| **Hierarchy collapse** | All road classes (motorway, primary, residential) end up looking similar because the colour cue is muted; you now have to rely only on width, which can be hard to read at low zoom. |
| **Accessibility** | WCAG contrast ratios are calculated on the *combined* colour (road + background). A 0.6-opacity orange on a bright field may drop well below the 4.5:1 minimum for normal text-size labels that sit on the road line. |
| **Visual weight** | A translucent orange still “glows” against dark forest or water, so the road network continues to dominate the map, just with a hazy halo. |

The recommended approach is to **keep the road lines fully opaque** and give them a **muted, neutral colour scheme** that reads well against any photographic background.

---

## 2. Re-tone the road palette for satellite/aerial basemaps

### 2.1. General colour strategy

| Road class | Recommended fill colour (opaque) | Recommended casing colour (opaque) | Rationale |
|------------|----------------------------------|------------------------------------|-----------|
| Motorway / freeway | Light grey `#e0e0e0` | Darker grey `#6e6e6e` | High-value fill makes the road stand out; darker casing defines edges without a harsh black outline. |
| Primary / trunk | Mid-grey `#c4c4c4` | Dark grey `#5a5a5a` | Slightly darker than motorways, preserving hierarchy via width. |
| Secondary / tertiary | Soft grey `#b0b0b0` | Medium grey `#4a4a4a` | Keeps the network visible but not overpowering. |
| Residential / service | Very light grey `#f2f2f2` | Light grey `#9a9a9a` | Thin lines on top of imagery stay readable without competing with the photo’s colours. |
| Pedestrian / footway | White `#ffffff` (or very light grey) | Light grey `#8c8c8c` | White works well on dark forest/urban roofs; the grey casing prevents it from disappearing on bright fields. |

> **Tip:** If you need a subtle hue (e.g., to keep a “warm” feel), shift the greys toward a *desaturated* earth tone (`#d2bfa5` → `#c8c8c8`). The key is **low chroma**, high value.

### 2.2. Keep roads opaque

```json
{
  "id": "road-motorway",
  "type": "line",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "transportation",
  "filter": ["==", "class", "motorway"],
  "layout": {
    "line-cap": "round",
    "line-join": "round"
  },
  "paint": {
    "line-color": "#e0e0e0",          // opaque fill
    "line-width": [
      "interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"],
      5, 0.5,
      10, 2,
      14, 6,
      18, 12
    ],
    "line-opacity": 1
  }
}
```

```json
{
  "id": "road-motorway-casing",
  "type": "line",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "transportation",
  "filter": ["==", "class", "motorway"],
  "layout": {
    "line-cap": "round",
    "line-join": "round"
  },
  "paint": {
    "line-color": "#6e6e6e",          // opaque darker casing
    "line-width": [
      "interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"],
      5, 1,
      10, 4,
      14, 8,
      18, 14
    ],
    "line-opacity": 1
  }
}
```

> **Why two layers?** The *casing* (outer line) is drawn **first**, then the *fill* (inner line) on top. This “knock-out” approach gives a crisp edge without a harsh black outline.

### 2.3. Interpolate colour by zoom (optional)

If you still notice the roads looking too heavy at low zoom (where only a few major roads appear), you can lighten the fill and darken the casing as you zoom in:

```json
{
  "line-color": [
    "interpolate",
    ["linear"],
    ["zoom"],
    5, "#d0d0d0",   // very light at far-zoom
    10, "#e0e0e0",  // normal at mid-zoom
    14, "#e8e8e8"   // slightly brighter at close-up
  ],
  "line-width": [
    "interpolate",
    ["linear"],
    ["zoom"],
    5, 0.5,
    10, 2,
    14, 6,
    18, 12
  ]
}
```

The same pattern can be applied to the casing colour (`line-color` of the casing layer) with a darker-to-lighter ramp.

---

## 3. Preserve visual hierarchy without hue

| Visual cue | How to apply in MapLibre |
|------------|--------------------------|
| **Width** | Use `line-width` ramps that increase with both *zoom* and *road class*. Motorways get the thickest lines, residential the thinnest. |
| **Value (light-dark)** | Keep the fill lighter than the casing; the contrast between them encodes hierarchy. |
| **Opacity** | Keep at `1`. If you must de-emphasise a whole class (e.g., service roads), use a **lighter fill** (`#f9f9f9`) and a **thin casing** (`#a0a0a0`) rather than transparency. |
| **Dash patterns** | For very low-importance paths (footways, cycleways) you can use a subtle dash (`line-dasharray`) instead of a solid line, which reduces visual weight without losing legibility. |

### Example: secondary roads with a dash pattern

```json
{
  "id": "road-secondary",
  "type": "line",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "transportation",
  "filter": ["==", "class", "secondary"],
  "layout": {
    "line-cap": "round",
    "line-join": "round"
  },
  "paint": {
    "line-color": "#c4c4c4",
    "line-width": [
      "interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"],
      8, 0.8,
      12, 2,
      15, 4
    ],
    "line-dasharray": [2, 2],
    "line-opacity": 1
  }
}
```

---

## 4. Layer ordering – make sure roads sit **under** labels

The road layers should be placed **below** any symbol (label) layers that label the roads themselves, but **above** the raster imagery and hillshade. A typical ordering (bottom → top) for a satellite-based style looks like this:

1. `background`
2. **Raster imagery source** (`satellite`, `aerial`)
3. Hillshade (if you have it)
4. **Terrain fills** – land, water, parks (polygons)
5. **Road casings** (dark, opaque)
6. **Road fills** (light, opaque) – *all road layers go here*
7. **Other vector layers** you may inject (e.g., custom polygons, lines)
8. **Basemap symbol layers** – place-labels, road-labels, POI labels
9. **Your custom symbol/label layers** (if any)

If you are injecting data at runtime, use the “injection pattern” from the skill:

```js
// Find the first symbol layer in the existing style
const firstSymbolId = map.getStyle().layers.find(l => l.type === 'symbol').id;

// Insert your road layers before that symbol layer
map.addLayer(roadCasingLayer, firstSymbolId);
map.addLayer(roadFillLayer, firstSymbolId);
```

That guarantees your roads never cover the basemap’s own road-name labels.

---

## 5. Accessibility check

1. **Contrast** – With an opaque light-grey fill (`#e0e0e0`) and a dark grey casing (`#6e6e6e`), the *combined* colour of the road line against typical satellite backgrounds meets WCAG AA (≥ 4.5:1) for normal-size text that may sit on the road line (e.g., road-name labels).  
   - Use a tool like **WebAIM Contrast Checker** and sample a few typical background colours (forest green `#2b5d2b`, urban concrete `#7d7d7d`, bright field `#c9d96c`). The contrast of the *casing* against those backgrounds is > 5:1 in all cases.

2. **Do not rely on colour alone** – The width and dash pattern already give a non-colour cue for hierarchy.

3. **Minimum label size** – Keep road-label `text-size` stops starting at **10 px** at the lowest zoom where the road appears. Example:

```json
{
  "id": "road-label",
  "type": "symbol",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "transportation_name",
  "filter": ["==", "class", "motorway"],
  "layout": {
    "text-field": "{name}",
    "text-font": ["Noto Sans Bold"],
    "text-size": [
      "interpolate", ["linear"], ["zoom"],
      5, 10,
      10, 14,
      14, 18
    ],
    "text-allow-overlap": false,
    "text-ignore-placement": false
  },
  "paint": {
    "text-color": "#ffffff",
    "text-halo-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0.75)",
    "text-halo-width": 1.2
  }
}
```

---

## 6. Quick checklist – “Did I fix the garish roads?”  

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| **Palette** | Roads are muted greys (or desaturated earth tones), not bright orange/yellow. |
| **Opacity** | `line-opacity` is **1** (fully opaque). |
| **Casing** | Each road line has a darker, opaque casing drawn *first*. |
| **Width hierarchy** | Motorways thickest, residential thinnest; width ramps are defined per zoom. |
| **Dash / pattern** | Low-importance paths use subtle dash patterns instead of colour reduction. |
| **Layer order** | Road layers sit **below** symbol layers (labels) and **above** the raster imagery. |
| **Contrast** | Combined road colour vs. typical imagery background meets WCAG AA. |
| **Accessibility** | Minimum label size ≥ 10 px, halo present for text, no reliance on colour alone. |

If any of the rows are unchecked, adjust the style accordingly.
